items.utterance: What would you do differently next time?
items.answer: Great question! Let me explain VAD and turn-taking : Detection runs in your browser, not on a server. An audio worklet downmixes the microphone, resamples it to sixteen kilohertz, and measures the loudness of every thirty-two millisecond frame. One loud frame means you have started, or three in a row while I am speaking, so a leak of my own voice cannot cut me off; six hundred milliseconds of quiet mean you have finished. Anything shorter than two hundred and fifty milliseconds is discarded as a misfire, so a cough or a keystroke never reaches the network, and three hundred milliseconds of audio from before the onset is kept so your first syllable is not clipped. Only the finished utterance is uploaded, which is one transcription request per turn rather than a permanent stream. Two honest caveats. Transcription cannot begin until you stop talking, which costs latency; in exchange, interruption is detected locally and needs no round trip at all. And this is an energy threshold, not a neural detector: a small model like Silero would tell speech from other sounds far better in a noisy room. That swap is one file, and it is on the list. Looking at slide 3 of 6: "Hearing: VAD and Turn-Taking" Next time, I would use a neural detector for better performance in noisy environments. But the current setup works well for most scenarios.
